[The Future of the Humanities - by Justin Smith-Ruiu](https://www.the-hinternet.com/p/the-future-of-the-humanities)

> For the past few years I have repeatedly characterized the state of university-based humanities research and education as “late-Soviet” (I believe I first borrowed this line from Stefan Collini, but may be misremembering). The actual period of reference, in my living memory, extends, let us say, from the Reykjavík Summit of October, 1986, to the official dissolution of the USSR on Boxing Day, 1991. When I have previously invoked the comparison, I have imagined that we were living roughly in the equivalent of 1987, when the system had already been greatly hollowed out, and virtually no one continued to believe in its official mission, but a typical apparatchik could still be expected reliably to show up at work for yet another day of make-believe. The present semester, Fall 2026, feels decidedly more like the late-late-Soviet period, after the fall of the Berlin Wall in November, 1989. Now we wake up each day wondering, with very good reason, whether _this_ will be the day we can finally stop pretending.

The Future of the Humanities - by Justin Smith-Ruiu

For the past few years I have repeatedly characterized the state of university-based humanities research and education as “late-Soviet” (I believe I first borrowed this line from Stefan Collini, but may be misremembering). The actual period of reference, in my living memory, extends, let us say, from the Reykjavík Summit of October, 1986, to the official dissolution of the USSR on Boxing Day, 1991. When I have previously invoked the comparison, I have imagined that we were living roughly in the equivalent of 1987, when the system had already been greatly hollowed out, and virtually no one continued to believe in its official mission, but a typical apparatchik could still be expected reliably to show up at work for yet another day of make-believe. The present semester, Fall 2026, feels decidedly more like the late-late-Soviet period, after the fall of the Berlin Wall in November, 1989. Now we wake up each day wondering, with very good reason, whether this will be the day we can finally stop pretending.
